Mined from 27 transcripts (~1.02M chars) pulled 2026-10-04 from _ingest/raw/2026-10-04/media/primary-vp/. Grouped by speaker: Brad Svrluga (co-founder; day-to-day managing partner): Unconventional Path EP 75 (Q1 2020) and EP 141 (mid-2022); Bloomberg Cornell Tech Series (early 2021); Post Money "Tank to a Knife Fight" (Fund V announcement day, Feb 2026); Mark Peter Davis "Gold Standard for Seed VC" (late 2025); Vintage 19th VC Summit "Next Gen Seed Platform" (2025); Primary NYC Summit 2025 with Martin Mignot (Index). Ben Sun (co-founder; co-CIO, LP fundraising lead): NY Seed Round "Seed to Series A" (~2023); NY Seed Round "How to Start a VC Fund" with Mar Hershenson of Pear (~2023); Grace Gong "World's Largest Seed Firm" (~2024); Human Unicorn Pod EP30 with Nihal Mehta (2025); Harlem Capital "Inside Primary VC: $1.65B AUM" (2025); Full Ratchet replay with Nick Moran (~2021); NYC Tech Awards 2025 closeout. Svrluga also: "Welcome to Primary's NYC Summit" (Sept 2023); Bloomberg Tech at the Primary Summit with Sun (2025). Partners and staff: Jason Shuman ×3 (Just Go Grind, ~2021; Christian D Evans, late 2022; Startups Decoded, ~2025); Brian Schechter (Vintage clip, ~2025); Sam Toole (Lynx Collective, ~2025); Cassie Young ×2 (Go1 L&D, Feb 2025; Revenue Leadership podcast "Are You Uninvestable?", 2026); Gina Yocum, director of talent (Uncubed, ~2019–20); Tobias Citron's CISO podcast with GitHub's CISO (Primary channel); "Fund V" launch video (Feb 2026). Used for Primary's role only: "The $40M Push To Modernize Fleet Payments" (Daniel Simon, Coast). Dates are inferred from on-tape cues. Summarized in own words with brief attributed quotes only; no passages reproduced. Courses mapped: Course 10 (Entrepreneurship & Venture), Exec E2 (Capital Allocation), Course 04 (Strategy: "scaled seed" as a positioning choice between boutique and multi-stage platform). Bias line: nearly every source is a fundraising-adjacent appearance (fund launches, LP-facing summits, podcasts hosted by friends, co-investors or Primary's own channel) and doubles as firm marketing. Performance figures are self-reported and unaudited. The Fund I "unicorn" count is a survivorship stat: it counts companies that reached a $1B valuation in some round (several during 2020–21), not realized exit value. Treat it as a leading indicator, not DPI. Press facts (from the brief, cited as "press"): founded 2015 in NYC by Svrluga and Sun; Fund III $150M (Feb 2021, TechCrunch); Sept 2022 $425M = $275M Fund IV + $150M Primary Select; Fund V $625M (Feb 2026), billed as the largest standalone seed firm, eight sector partners, impact team 60+ heading to ~80, PrimaryLabs incubation; firm-reported Fund I: 9 of 25 unicorns plus 2 more exits above $500M.

What this adds over harlem capital vc insights

The sibling note covers the allocator's seat through an emerging-manager mission fund: Harlem started as a $25k angel LLC, runs lean ("minimize headcount, maximize AUM"), and uses media as its leverage. It pitches a diversity inefficiency, runs a generalist book diversified across 10 dimensions, and grew into a $134M Fund II. Primary is the opposite bet on the same 2015 NYC starting line. It treats seed as an industrialized market that can absorb a $425M+ seed vehicle, and splits the investment team into sector specialists who each run a ~$50M book. It spends most of its management fee on a 60-person operating company: recruiters, pipeline-generating BDRs, strategic finance, and an incubation studio. Harlem's edge is access and trust in an overlooked founder pool. Primary's is capacity: it hires headcount to raise its seed-to-A graduation rate and to win competitive rounds. The Harlem note already holds a second-hand Ben Sun profile (§11). This note works from the primary sources, adds Svrluga's fund-design logic, and checks the numbers against each other.

1 · Why "scaled seed": the strategy and its origin

  • Positioning as a Goldilocks middle. Svrluga frames founders' choice as a boutique seed firm (2–3 generalist partners, thin resources) versus a multi-stage platform that will promise resources but has misaligned incentives on a $5M round out of a $5B fund. A seed check is option value to a mega-fund, which may back competitors and index across a category. Primary claims the middle: stage-dedicated, but staffed like a platform. He calls it the "preeminent institutional-grade seed firm."
  • The barbell he is arguing against. At the 2025 Summit he cited the consensus view that venture is splitting into mega-platforms and niche players, with the middle as a death zone. His figures: ~58% of all VC dollars raised the prior year went to nine firms, and first-time funds fell ~60%. In 2022 he invoked the JCPenney analogy (stuck between boutiques and Walmart) for undifferentiated mid-size firms. Primary's answer is to be a specialist platform, not a scaled generalist.
  • Seed as a big enough market (Sun's "billion-dollar seed fund" manifesto, written ~2019–20). US seed went from ~$3B to ~$15B a year over ten years (his figures; the Harlem note quotes $5B to $20B). The arithmetic: put ~60% of $1B into seed over 3 years and you write ~$200M of seed checks a year, which is ~1.3% of the market. At $280M (Fund IV) it was ~$60M a year, under 1%. His conclusion is that "too big for seed" is a myth when measured against the market.
  • Only ~150 seed deals a year matter. Of ~5,000 US seed deals, ~3% historically become unicorns, so ~150 drive returns. Thousands of firms now compete for them in an efficient market, where a founder who changes a LinkedIn title to "stealth" gets dozens of inbound messages. Scale, in this view, is how you win your share of those 150.
  • Origin: NYC as the first wedge. In 2013–14 the biggest NYC tech exit was Tumblr ($1B). Sun's thesis was that NYC had always attracted talent, but that talent was not working on startups until the financial crisis pushed ~200K finance workers out. A Midas-list VC told him a NYC-only seed fund was "insane." Primary invested almost only in NYC for 5–6 years. Svrluga: "we defined a battle we could win." Narrowing made the story credible to LPs and made the operating model possible: every portfolio company was within 20–30 minutes of the office.
  • Earning the right to stretch. The geographic alpha disappeared around 2019–20. Sun says they stopped seeing and winning every NYC deal they wanted, because markets are more efficient than people think. They moved from a geographic edge to a structural one (specialists plus platform). By ~2024 most deals in the current fund were outside NYC: Bay Area, Chicago, Boston, Israel.
  • Svrluga's general lesson: pick what you want to be known for and say no to whole customer segments. "Give yourself the advice you would give a portfolio company."

Applies when the seed market is large and growing, and founders value stage-dedicated help over brand-name multi-stage optionality. Breaks when seed volume shrinks (a post-bubble contraction) or multi-stage firms credibly commit resources at seed, which collapses the middle.

2 · Fund size → ownership → the return-the-fund math (worked from the tapes)

The fund ladder, from transcripts and press:

Fund Size Source / note
I (closed Feb 2015) $60M Svrluga; 2-year raise (late 2013 to mid-2015)
II $100M Svrluga, Bloomberg 2021
III (2021) $150M (press, Bloomberg) / "$155M" (Svrluga, 2022) small on-tape discrepancy
IV + Select (2022) $275M + $150M (press); Sun on tape: "$280M seed fund," "$275M seed + $150M select"
V + Select (2026) $625M total (press, Fund V video) Svrluga on announcement day: "$425M seed + $225M select" (sums to $650M); Sun on Harlem's channel (2025): current fund "close to $650M"; Sun elsewhere: seed fund "$415M" and "8 check-writers of a $450M fund"; Shuman: "Fund V core and Select IV." Two tapes point to ~$650M; the 2026 Cassie Young podcast intro (host's words) says "$625M seed fund." Unreconciled; use the $625M headline.

AUM claims drift the same way: "$1B" (Sun ~2024; Cassie Young Feb 2025), "a little over $1B" (Shuman ~2025, before Fund V), "over a billion raised over the decade" (Sun), and "$1.6B" (Sun himself on Harlem Capital's channel, 2025).

Worked math, as Svrluga gave it: - 2020, $100M fund (Fund II). Take $15–20M off the top for fees and costs, leaving ~$80–90M invested. If a third goes to zero and a third returns ~2x, the remaining third (~$30M) must produce ~$270–300M by itself. So winners need roughly 10x. The house rule: no deal unless it can return the whole fund on its own. At 10–15% ownership over time, that means a $700M to $1.5B outcome. - 2022, $150M fund (Fund III). First checks ran $0.5M to $4–5M, sweet spot $3–3.5M. The bar fell to "can return half the fund in one shot." That means $75–80M of proceeds, so a $250M exit would need 30% ownership, which no founder will sell. Target markets are therefore $2B+, and bigger still for capital-intensive businesses, because the next investor writing a $50M check may need a $10B market. Ownership target: 15–20% at entry. Pricing: underwrite a 3x step-up to the next round (pay $20M post, expect $60M+ pre). - Why syndicates broke down. Splitting a $4M round three ways leaves a $1.3M check. Even a 20x on that returns $26M, which is not enough for a $155M fund. Every growing firm needs bigger checks, so the old Primary/First Round/Lerer three-way co-investing ended. - Sun's per-partner reframe. The Floodgate-era rule ("each deal can return the fund") assumed 2 partners on a $30–40M fund. With 8 check-writers, each partner controls ~12% of the fund. The right test is whether each partner's ~$50M book can return 5x+. His figures: $280M ÷ 6 ≈ $47M; ~$450M ÷ 8 ≈ $52–53M. That is roughly a solo GP's fund, but with ~10 staff behind each partner. He pitches it to LPs as "eight 5x funds." - Sun's unicorn-rate rule. At current prices you need about 10% of seed bets to become unicorns for a 3x+ net fund. Decacorns are only ~5% of ~1,500 private unicorns (~70–80), so you cannot count on one. Check: Fund I's claimed 9/25 is 36% (Svrluga said "38% or 40%"), more than three times that bar. Sun, in 2025, said "half a dozen" of 25; on Harlem's channel he said 8 unicorns from ~35 deals across Funds I–II. - Shuman's incubation lever on the same math. At 10–15% ownership you need a unicorn rate above 10% to return the fund. Incubation buys higher ownership, which he says lowers the bar to about 7.5%, or lets a $1B exit do the work of a $2B one. That is the financial case for the ~30% of deals that are homegrown. - Svrluga's scaling warning: AUM per partner, not AUM. When AUM per partner grows faster than average round size at your stage, returns fall. Partners drift later, become less price-sensitive, and hunt for places to put $15M to work. Adding check-writers without a way to keep decision quality up also degrades returns. Primary's answer is to hold capital per partner roughly flat (about $50–70M, adjusted for bigger seed rounds), add specialist partners, and let the platform lift each partner's hit rate.

Applies when ownership stays at 10–20% and each partner's book is roughly solo-GP sized. Breaks when round sizes inflate faster than books ("outrageous $50M seeds"), which forces either lower ownership or drift into later rounds, or when headline fund growth outruns the number of credible check-writers.

3 · Primary Select: an opportunity fund, not a continuation vehicle

  • What it is. A separate pool ($150M in 2022 per press; "$225M" alongside Fund V per Svrluga) that writes larger follow-on checks into existing portfolio companies only. Sun: no new names. Press says follow-ons run up to Series A; Svrluga in 2026 described "later rounds of our best performing companies."
  • What it is not. A GP-led continuation vehicle (see wss private markets wealth §5) moves assets the GP already owns out of an old fund into a new vehicle. A secondary buyer prices them, and existing LPs can cash out. Its purpose is liquidity and extending the hold. Select does the reverse: it puts new primary capital into new financing rounds of companies the seed fund still holds. No asset changes hands between Primary vehicles, and no LP gets liquidity. It is a reserves strategy carved out into its own vehicle.
  • Sun's case for it: two products with different risk/return profiles. The core seed fund is the "high beta product": high conviction, high loss rate, multiple-driven. Select concentrates capital behind breakouts. It gets lower multiples but better IRR. Its claimed edge is access (pro-rata rights, board seats, founder relationships) plus insight (inside information on which companies the market is underpricing).
  • The reserves lesson behind it (Sun, "How to Start a VC Fund"). Early on they copied the conventional 1:1 reserves ratio without asking why. They then watched follow-on rounds get crowded and repriced, and concluded they should have bought more at entry, at roughly a quarter of the price. They changed course mid-Fund I. Splitting out Select lets the seed fund spend more on initial ownership while the follow-on decision gets its own capital and its own LP underwriting.
  • Inference (mine, not on tape): the obvious conflict to watch is cross-fund pricing. Fund A's portfolio is marked by the round that Fund B (Select) helps fill. That is benign when an outside lead sets the price and Select only takes pro-rata. It is a real agency issue if Select leads insider rounds. The transcripts do not say how Select's pricing is governed. n/d.

Applies when the GP has genuine inside information and an outside lead prices the round. Breaks when Select becomes a way to defend marks on struggling companies, or when the access edge weakens because hot companies cut pro-rata.

4 · Sector specialization: "no place for generalists"

  • How the model emerged (Svrluga). Around 2019 the firm needed two things at once. Strong internal hires needed a checkbook or they would leave (one did). And the competitor he feared most was the niche micro-fund that does nothing but one sector all day. Winning a fintech deal against a fintech-only investor was harder than beating a generalist, even though he had two fintech-infrastructure unicorns in Fund I. So the firm specialized at the level of each individual partner.
  • The roster on tape: Sam Toole (healthcare), Emily Man (fintech/financial services; the one external partner hire, from Redpoint), Tobias Citron (cybersecurity), Brian Schechter (compute and infrastructure software; runs Primary Labs), Jason Shuman (consumer/fintech/proptech/marketplaces in 2021–22), and Cassie Young (go-to-market; oversees the impact team). The Fund V video adds semiconductors/AI infrastructure. Count: seven partners (late 2025); "eight partner check-writers" (Sun, 2025); eight sector partners (press).
  • The job definition. Each specialist's goal is to be one of the two or three best seed investors in their sector in the world. Svrluga says that goal is impossible if you also have to stay inside NYC, which is why specialization forced geographic expansion.
  • Governance: a "miniature fund of funds." Each partner runs a fairly independent book. Svrluga and Sun share the CIO role and a technical IC, but Sun says the IC works as a veto that has never been used. They let partners do deals they would personally have voted against; some of those became the biggest winners.
  • Why specialists underwrite better (Sun). Series A investors are now sector-specialized. A seed firm is in an "origination business" and has to know what its buyer will want. Emily Man came from the A-round buyer side and knew which fintech models A investors avoid (e.g., lending), which suits Sun's internal target of getting 80% of seed bets to an A.
  • Partner pipeline. Most partners were promoted from within. Trust built over 3–5 years of watching someone work beats six months of dinners. Svrluga: "You have to lose money before you can learn how to make money" — give people the checkbook before you are sure they are ready, and tolerate the losses that build negative pattern recognition.
  • Contrast inside the sources: Index's Martin Mignot defended a generalist partnership. Index staffs each deal with a team based on relationship, proximity and expertise, and its eight fund-returners came from seven different partners. Specialization is one valid answer, not the only one.

Applies when downstream investors are sector-specialized and the sector has enough deal volume to fill a partner's book. Breaks when a sector cools (Primary largely exited consumer after 6–8 bad years) and a specialist's book gets stuck in a dead category, or when the best deals cut across categories.

5 · The impact team as product: cost, funding, and whether it shows up in returns

  • Headcount trajectory (on tape): 18 people (Q1 2020, already far larger than peers' 4–5) → 32–33, more than half on impact (2022) → ~50, about a third investors (2023–24; Sam Toole: 13 investors and 30+ on the portfolio) → 60, investment team under a third (2025–26) → 75–80 by end of 2026. Fund V video: "scaling to an 80-person team."
  • What the team does. It started with talent (one person on day one). Then it added strategic finance (models, KPIs, data-room prep for the A; separate from fund admin), then go-to-market and market development. The People & Networks group, led by Rebecca Price, has 9–10 full-time recruiters. They placed a 160th hire by mid-year 2025 and were on track for ~180–190 (Sun); the Harlem note says 170 the prior year. Recruiters report cold-outreach connect rates 3–6x higher than at brand-name startups. The market development group is a half-dozen to 8 BDR-style associates who book customer meetings for portfolio companies; the Fund V video claims 1,300 meetings and $30M of qualified pipeline; Shuman cites 1,000+ sales meetings set up in a year. Cassie Young (ex-CRO of a ~$200M ARR SaaS company) oversees the whole function, with three former executives running its pillars (~35 people, ~2025).
  • Service ratios on purpose (Shuman). The impact team has grown faster than the portfolio, because one market-dev rep can serve maybe 5–10 companies a month before quality drops. He contrasts this with platform teams nominally serving 1,200 companies. Primary avoids the word "platform" for that reason. Cadence: a monthly line-by-line review of every portfolio company with the impact team, built around each company's one or two "glass balls" (the things it cannot drop), plus Slack channels for hires landed and customer wins. By 2026 the go-to-market practice (run by Jason Gelman) had added a go-to-market engineering team for portfolio companies (Cassie Young).
  • How it is paid for. Mostly from management fees, which is the point. Sun says a fee base on ~$1B AUM makes running a firm "very profitable." If they cut half the team, LPs would barely notice, and the partners would keep the money. Instead: "let's put the fees on the field." Svrluga describes years of sacrificed current compensation. Sun cites Bezos's "your margin is my opportunity." The stated alignment logic is to earn money from carry, not fees, so the partners do not become dependent on fees and turn risk-averse (host Nihal Mehta's gloss, which Sun endorsed).
  • What portfolio companies pay. Recruiting is the only charged service: about 20–25% of the cost of an outside recruiter, run at a loss. They charge so companies take it seriously. Customer development is mostly free. Nothing is mandatory, and companies can fire Primary and get their money back (Svrluga says nobody ever has).
  • The KPI pivot. Once the firm was ~60% non-investors, the impact team drifted toward measuring NPS, the natural metric for a professional-services group. Leadership pulled it back to the only metric that matters to LPs, MOIC. Recruiters now explain their work in terms of value created for the deal partner's companies, and the team withdraws resources from companies that are not working.
  • Avoiding adverse selection. Svrluga: build the capabilities to attract the founders who need them least. Compensating for a weak founder with services is a losing strategy. Utilization is highest among experienced repeat founders.
  • Does it show up in returns? The evidence offered is all self-reported:
  • Seed-to-Series-A graduation. "90% raise an outside-led A" (2021); "over 90% vs 25–30% industry" (Sun). Sun says this, not picking skill, drives the unicorn hit rate: he could not predict unicorns a decade out, but he could underwrite to the A.
  • Fund ranks. Fund I "top 5%" (Svrluga) vs "top 1%" (Sun); "two top-5% global funds" (Shuman, 2022). Svrluga said in 2022 that Funds I and II each held multiple companies valued above the entire fund.
  • Size vs returns. Sun argues that fund size matters less than stage: small funds look better in rankings because early-stage returns are widely dispersed. He says the prior fund, already top-5% by seed-fund size, is on track to be Primary's best. Shuman's version is that the partners would not divert money from their own pockets without seeing a return. Both are assertions, not evidence.
  • No counterfactual. There is no matched comparison of supported vs unsupported companies. Founder selection and service intensity are confounded. The impact team's sourcing value (recruiters asking candidates who will found next) is another unpriced channel.
  • Cultural cost. It is an operating company with HR issues, budgets, KPI screens on the walls and pod plans. Svrluga says name-brand VCs tell him they would not want his job.

Applies when fees are large enough to fund senior operators, and portfolio companies are at the stage where recruiting and first pipeline are the binding constraints. Breaks when fees shrink (a smaller fund or a fee holiday), when growth-stage investors do not take over and Primary ends up serving B-stage companies, or when the team optimizes service metrics instead of MOIC.

6 · Sourcing and the NYC ecosystem machine

  • The shift in sourcing channels. In ~2015–16, 30–50% of deals came from other investors' referrals. By 2021 it was ~10% (Shuman). Early on the "hitch your wagon" strategy meant regular check-ins with the ~10 established NYC firms (First Round, Greycroft, Lerer) to stay in their deal flow. Sun says a new fund today needs its own sourcing edge. He has also argued there is no longer proprietary deal flow: nearly every deal has multiple term sheets, so the skill that matters is winning. ~2021 KPI: a 90% win-rate target on issued term sheets, running mid-to-high 80s. The win pitch brings the whole team (around 22 people at the time) with a customized deck naming candidate hires and target customers.
  • Talent tracking before ideas exist. Specialists track the best people in their sectors, watch vesting schedules, and ask who would back whom with personal money. Sun asks strong operators for "the three best people you ever worked with" and builds a network of high-signal people inside NYC's scaled startups (Warby Parker and similar). Shuman knew one Dandy co-founder for 8–9 years before backing him. Svrluga: if you wait for deals to be shopped, "you've already lost."
  • Incubation as sourcing and cost basis. It started on the side of Sun's desk in Fund I, and was hidden from LPs because it looked odd. It became ~30% of deals, run by a dozen-person team (Primary Labs, led by Schechter) that spins out 4+ companies a year. LPs now cite it as a reason to invest. The model hands strong operators an idea and a check on the day they quit. The first two incubations were worth over $1B combined (2022). Incubation seed rounds averaged more than $5M at more than a $20M valuation even in the 2022 bear market. Sun compares it to YC: proprietary deal flow at a low cost basis. Variant: Coast's founder got a desk at Primary before he had an idea, with a promise that Primary would put in the first money.
  • Ecosystem assets as top of funnel. The NYC Summit started to fix a brand problem: a Sand Hill investor had asked one of their founders who Primary was. They solved it by offering West Coast VCs stage time. Svrluga's 2023 welcome dates the first edition to 2017 (150 people) and put the fifth at ~2,000. In 2025 he said 2016, nine editions and ~3,000; Sun said ~2,000 invite-only in its ninth year. Specialists also run buyer-facing content: Tobias Citron's CISO interview series tells founders how security buyers evaluate startups. Also: NYC Tech Awards (Kevin Ryan the first Hall of Fame inductee), NYC Founders Guide, a 15-person Founders Fellowship, a Future Founders program, and the Factor nonprofit (first cohort of 20, placing underrepresented talent into startups; Harlem Capital is a named partner). Recruiters double as sourcing scouts.
  • Volume and selectivity:
  • 2020: ~1,000 opportunities a year, 250–400 looked at closely, 7–10 investments.
  • ~2024 (Sun): each partner sees ~100 funded seed deals a year and does 2–3. Firm-wide, more than 900 closed seed deals were reviewed and 9 term sheets issued (under 1%).
  • Pipeline metric. Primary counts deals that actually raised, not decks received, to grade a partner's coverage.
  • NYC coverage. It saw ~70% of NYC seed deals over three years.
  • Scaled research tools. An internal expert network of ~3,500 people gives a partner deal context within 24–48 hours. Marketing "air cover" (outbound tech, events and content production) runs on demand. Sun also co-founded Altus, a private-company research firm incubated with an ex-BCG partner as CEO. His model is the pre-meeting research Tiger Global bought from Bain, sold as "market beta" to all investors. He cites PitchBook's growth from $30M to $700M ARR as the market-size precedent.
  • The NYC scorecard (Sun): 3 private unicorns ~10 years ago vs ~150 now (~200 by his 2025 Bloomberg count), which he says is more than the next ten markets combined (Miami has 6). There have been 50+ NYC tech IPOs since 2019, and NYC tech employs 500–600K people vs ~1M in the Bay Area. NYC now does ~1,000 seed deals a year to the Bay Area's ~1,200, and took 15% of VC dollars vs 23% for the Bay Area. Svrluga's B2B argument: no other market gives you as many customers within reach (finance, media, advertising, pharma, CPG). His 2023 Summit figures: 1 in 17 NYC workers is in tech vs 1 in 4 in the Bay Area, and NYC has ~70% more Fortune 500 headquarters across twice as many industries.

Applies when the firm can build sourcing that compounds (talent graphs, incubation, events) instead of relying on referrals. Breaks when the geography is fully covered by every multi-stage firm (true of NYC since ~2019), so the edge has to move from where you invest to what you bring.

7 · The seed-to-A bar: what founders must prove

  • Underwrite to the Series A, not to the unicorn (Sun). Seed capital buys 18–24 months of runway. Work out what A investors in that category require (customers, revenue, product state, team), underwrite the team's ability to hit it, then use the impact team to help them get there. Raise at least six months before cash-out (Shuman).
  • Concrete A thresholds (Shuman, late 2022): a 3x markup at the A is the target. For SaaS that usually means $1–2M ARR with a clear path to tripling within a year. Consumer subscription companies now need more like $5–10M ARR. Unit economics should be profitable after the A. If you raised at a $1B peak valuation and the market halved, you need 2x+ growth just to grow back into your price.
  • When Primary doubles down (Svrluga): before revenue gets large, once product-market fit shows. His example: $200K revenue in July grew to $2.5M+ run-rate nine months later, with 50 customers. The test is whether downstream investors will look at the company and want to pile in.
  • Founder screens, consistent across speakers. The founder matters most; Svrluga says he has relearned this every year for 25 years. His "three unnatural sales": recruiting employees into a likely failure, raising money from investors who expect to lose it, and getting a customer to bet their job and mortgage on a startup. Sun's version is "wait for great": would you bet against this person at anything, even French cooking? Sam Toole looks for rate of learning. Shuman checks how fast a founder answers email during a raise, and what they learned between month 0 and month 12. Non-obvious deals need numbers "popping off the page" (Sun). Sun's weighting (~2021): founder 80–90%, market 10–20%. Tailwind markets are the "wet sponge" versus a rock. If the firm loves the founder but disagrees with the business model, it passes and stays close in case of a pivot. He also tells founders to spend at least half their energy on distribution, not the 90/10 product/distribution split that worked for him in 1997.
  • The "future equity story" (Shuman, ~2025). Between rounds, the deal partner and the founder write down what the company should look like to Series A investors 8–14 months out, and the milestones to get there. Shuman pressure-tests these narratives with ~40 later-stage firms because the AI-era goalposts keep moving.
  • Failure modes Primary tries to prevent:
  • Bad first hires. Two wrong hires at a two-founder company can cost a year, and reaching the A with no product shipped is fatal.
  • Late leadership build-out. Founders settle for "good" hires; Primary shows them a great exemplar they cannot yet hire, to calibrate.
  • Doing too much. Insecure founders try 20 things to land 2 and land none.
  • Boards: ~50% of seed rounds now get a formal board. Svrluga says governance fights at seed mean "you've already lost." What matters is a quarterly step-back with goals (OKRs or anything else), one-page pre-reads, and under 90 minutes. Tactical product and branding debates belong in working sessions, not board meetings.
  • Where the playbook does not fit (Sam Toole): healthcare care-delivery companies often cannot show results within 18–24 months. They may need to raise more up front, or from alternative capital. Primary avoids FDA-path companies.

Applies when A investors have legible, category-specific bars the seed firm can reverse-engineer. Breaks when A rounds become momentum-priced (2021) or freeze (2022), so the target moves mid-runway, or in capital-intensive categories where 18–24 months cannot reach the proof point.

8 · Markups vs DPI, exits, the LP base, and the post-2021 market

  • Exits named on tape (Fund I): Mirror, ~$500M to Lululemon (2020), the first material exit. An unnamed consumer company sold for ~$800M at roughly 20-something times invested capital (early 2026). Alma, announced sale to Spring Health (pending, early 2026). Eight Fund I companies passed $100M revenue. Other names: Alloy, Vestwell (fintech infrastructure), Jet.com, Latch (SPAC), K Health, Slice (>$100M net revenue), and Dandy (Fund II; pivoted from aligners into dental labs; 700+ people). Press adds "two more exits above $500M." No DPI figure appears on any tape.
  • Markups vs DPI. The firm's public metric is the unicorn count, which is a markup metric. Svrluga's 2022 claim that several companies were valued above the fund size is also about marks. The DPI discipline in this note comes from outside voices (see harlem capital vc insights §13, Lerer's "3-fund hump"). One honest data point: Svrluga's survival bar is that average VC firms return less than the S&P 500. Secondaries: not discussed on any tape (n/d).
  • Loss-rate drift (by date): "a third to zero" (2020, 2022); "25–50%" per wire (2021); "40, 50, 60%" and "60% of the time" (2026). This matches his AI-era view in §9 of higher failure rates with bigger outliers.
  • LP base: foreign sovereign wealth funds, university endowments and West Coast foundations (Bloomberg 2021). Vintage, a fund-of-funds, was the first institutional LP (Vintage summit). Fund I's tipping point was a single ~$2M family-office commitment. Today's largest LPs are $100B+ institutions with $30–50M per fund family. Svrluga says they want $500M+ over time and underwrite a 15–20-year relationship. Fund I was raised under the old High Peaks name because the largest LP could get "fund three of the old thing" through its committee more easily than a new brand; they renamed after the first capital call.
  • LP fundraising craft (Sun and Svrluga):
  • The LP memo. Give the LP a differentiated "why you win" story it can write into its memo. Do what you said you would do; strategy drift is a common LP complaint.
  • GP referrals. Ask well-regarded co-investors for LP introductions, and brief those GPs on your strategy (Sun did this with Thrive's Josh Kushner).
  • Tourist LPs. Sun spoke to ~100 LPs in one year and treats LPs who are new to venture or "switching strategy" as a red flag.
  • Allocation squeeze (Mar Hershenson). Seed managers are squeezed because ~80% of many LPs' venture budget goes to multi-stage firms. Sun saw LPs correcting back toward early stage (~2023).
  • Market-cycle reads:
  • Mid-2022 (Svrluga): public markets had corrected and growth investors had repriced, but seed "hasn't gotten the memo." He predicted seed repricing within ~6 months.
  • 2021, speed as a weapon (Sun): using fast closes to win deals was dangerous, because the diligence that matters is time with the founder.
  • 2025–26 (Svrluga): pricing doubles week to week. The OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX IPOs will cool the market if they trade poorly and heat it if they trade well.
  • Brand compounding (Sun, quoting an LP): venture is the one asset class that is not a random walk, because brand compounds.

Applies when LPs underwrite multi-fund relationships and accept marks as interim evidence. Breaks when the distribution drought (wss private markets wealth §6) forces LPs to rank managers on DPI, which the unicorn count does not show.

9 · AI's effect on seed: competition, capital intensity, compute bets

  • Opportunity (Svrluga, 2026): every industry is being turned over by startups, and large software incumbents cannot reinvent themselves fast enough. "Software as work" opens markets that were hard to sell into. Example: sell a landscaper or electrician software that comes with agents to run it, instead of a scheduling tool nobody wants to learn.
  • Threat: the most competition he has seen in any market. Every "off the beaten path" idea has five rivals. Incumbency cycles are compressing, so founders must build for model capabilities 12–24 months out or a newer startup will do to them what they are doing to incumbents. Founder quality matters ~"10 times" more. He sees no general shift to winner-take-all, except where a hard-to-copy data advantage exists.
  • Portfolio response: Fund V will hold more companies than any prior fund. The reason is more check-writers, not bigger checks. His view: failure rates go up and outliers get bigger, so more shots on goal make sense.
  • Capital intensity and the stack (Schechter): value will accrue across the whole stack: compute, models (DeepSeek reopened the model layer), middleware and applications. Vertical AI now delivers services, not just software. Hence specialization by layer and sector, and the Fund V semiconductors/AI-infrastructure partner.
  • The compute bet. Svrluga said the firm's most valuable company (2025) was a chip company started by two Harvard sophomores building an ASIC. It had ~$1.25B of pre-orders 2.5 years in, before shipping. He called it an "utterly absurd proposition" that was likely to lose money. He did not name it on tape; the description matches Etched, as the brief anticipates. He used it to argue that the best venture deals are often the ones most likely to fail.
  • AI-substitution diligence (Cassie Young, 2026). She now passes on companies she would have backed a year ago when buyers on her reference calls say they would try the product but could probably build it themselves with Claude. Her concern is that ARR traction arrives but nothing defensible remains afterward. Point solutions are most exposed. Her test is whether the domain needs purpose-built, deterministic accuracy (fund administration, supply-chain operations research) and whether the company has a credible path from point solution to platform. Go-to-market tools must hit one of her PRIME levers (productivity, retention, investment efficiency, momentum, expense reduction) or she will not invest. At seed she tolerates ugly burn multiples if there is a plan to bring them down. Revenue per employee now appears in Series A board decks, where it never used to. Both founders frame AI as infrastructure ("like electricity"), not a sector. Sun's caveat: today's bigger rounds and prices only work if AI produces bigger exits.
  • Consumer AI: apart from OpenAI, consumer AI has not happened yet, which is backwards relative to past platform shifts. Mignot's explanation is that ChatGPT absorbs most use cases; he expects room in high-liability verticals.
  • AI inside the firm (Sun, Harlem's channel): a four-person "Primary OS" team builds sourcing agents that watch LinkedIn, GitHub, papers, competitions and other VCs' interest. The go-to-market team builds a working customer-sourcing app for each finalist during the win process, e.g., mining Google reviews to rank home-services prospects. Sun's point is that a subscale firm cannot afford that team.
  • Round inflation (Shuman, ~2025): AI-era founders treat the next three years as a gold rush and raise much larger early rounds, "because they can." Multi-stage firms write seed checks as option bets. His analogy: if a $35M house and a $2M house are both on fire, you save the big one first.

Applies when AI lowers the cost of building, which raises the number of companies and the size of outliers. Breaks when AI raises capital needs at seed (compute, $50M+ seeds) beyond a ~$50M partner book, or when competition compresses outcomes so the bigger-outlier assumption fails.

10 · How Ben Sun describes starting a fund

  • Pre-history. Merrill Lynch tech banking (around the Netscape IPO), then founded Community Connect (AsianAvenue, BlackPlanet) in 1996–97. He bootstrapped it for two years, raised ~$20M, survived the dot-com crash, reached profitability with ~130–150 staff, and sold in early 2008 (Bear Stearns, his banker, collapsed mid-deal). His first backer, Bob Goldhammer, invested on the person, not the business. That shaped Sun's "betting on people betting on themselves" view.
  • Angel phase as the track record. At the end of 2009 he set aside "a couple million" and did ~10 deals in 4–5 years, often joining the board or co-founding. Four became unicorns, including Coupang (pickup basketball at Stuyvesant; ~$50M via SPVs and over $1B returned at IPO; market cap quoted at $30–75B depending on date). By ~2023 his lifetime record was 40 deals and 8 unicorns. The incubation habit started here, under an entity called Launch Time. He spun up a Groupon-style deals business for parents with two engineers and a PM, sold deals to merchants himself, and got distribution through Diapers.com via Marc Lore. Coupang came out of explaining that model to Bom Kim.
  • The founder record he invests from. At Community Connect, ad revenue could not sustain the business after 2000. He added paid dating profiles on top of the free social network in 2001, reaching ~$20M revenue and ~$6M EBITDA. The company sold to Radio One in 2008, and he says seed investors made ~30x.
  • Why institutionalize: he could not scale as one person, it was lonely, and the platform he wanted needed management fees. Svrluga wrote a public blog post listing seven partner attributes, held 125 coffee meetings, and asked Sun about six times. They wrote down shared core values first. Their "how" and "what" differ constantly, but the "why" does not.
  • Division of labor: co-CEOs for about five years. At ~20 people Sun handed the CEO role to Svrluga. Sun now does partner mentoring, "R&D" (incubation and experiments), and LP fundraising; he led the latest raise. Succession is planned 6–10 years out, and Svrluga says the "vast majority" of firm economics is already held by people other than the two founders.
  • His advice to new GPs: think from first principles rather than copying norms (the 1:1 reserves mistake). Run experiments even when LPs do not understand them yet (incubation). Start with a sourcing edge. Know your "why me." Svrluga adds: you do not have to compete for every deal.

Applies when the would-be GP has a founder-grade or angel-grade track record and a structural idea LPs can memo. Breaks when the "edge" is only a temporary market inefficiency, like NYC in 2015. Sun says that kind of alpha disappears fast.

The sharpest contrast: both firms treat the management fee as the strategic variable, and spend it in opposite ways. Harlem keeps headcount low and gets leverage from media and community (scalable, near-zero marginal cost). Primary turns fees into ~60 salaried operators and bets that services raise graduation rates and win rates enough to beat the drag of a bigger fund. Harlem's risk is capacity: a few partners cannot cover a growing fund. Primary's risk is fee dependence: the model needs fee-scale AUM, which requires either strong DPI or a fundraising market that funds "largest seed firm" stories.

Retrieval questions

  1. Why did Primary limit itself to NYC for its first 5–6 years? It made a credible, winnable story for LPs and let the services model work at short distances. Svrluga: "we defined a battle we could win."
  2. Svrluga's 2020 return-the-fund arithmetic for a $100M fund? Net out $15–20M of fees, assume a third to zero and a third at 2x, and the last ~$30M must make ~$300M, so ~10x winners. Every deal must be able to return the fund.
  3. How does Primary Select differ from a GP-led continuation vehicle? Select puts new capital into new rounds of current portfolio companies (no new names). A CV moves existing assets into a new vehicle to give LPs liquidity.
  4. What is Sun's per-partner reframe of fund size? Divide the fund by its check-writers: ~$50M each, like a solo GP with ~10 staff. Judge each book on 5x+, not whether every deal can return the whole fund.
  5. What unicorn rate does Sun say a seed fund needs? About 10% of seed bets for a 3x+ net fund, since only ~5% of unicorns become decacorns. Fund I's claimed 9/25 is 36%. Shuman: higher ownership via incubation cuts the bar to ~7.5%.
  6. How is the impact team funded, and what do companies pay? Mostly management fees ("put the fees on the field"). Only recruiting is charged, at ~20–25% of outside cost and run at a loss.
  7. What KPI correction did the impact team go through? It drifted toward NPS, a service metric, and was reoriented to MOIC on the deal partners' companies, with resources pulled from companies that are not working.
  8. Shuman's Series A bars (late 2022)? A 3x step-up. For SaaS, $1–2M ARR with a path to tripling. For consumer subscription, more like $5–10M ARR. Profitable unit economics after the A.
